articles.title: Google Messages could soon make pinned chats better with a clever layout switching trick
articles.excerpt: You may soon be able to pin more than six chats again and the layout will switch automatically.
articles.body: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority TL;DR Google Messages could soon automatically switch pinned chats between grid and list layouts based on how many chats you pin. The new tile layout could remain available for smaller collections of pinned chats, while the traditional list view could return when you pin more conversations. The change could also restore support for more than six pinned chats, although the strings don’t confirm whether Google will bring back the previous 20-chat limit. Google Messages recently introduced a redesigned pinned chats UI that replaces the traditional list of pinned chats with large, circular contact icons. While the new look makes pinned conversations easier to spot, it also comes with a limitation restricts you from pinning more than six chats.

articles.body: Alibaba's Qwen team dropped a new flagship today: Qwen4-Max, built on a brand-new Qwen4 architecture with a 2.4-trillion-parameter backbone, native vision, and a one-million-token context window. The headline number, though, is not the parameter count. It is the price: on Qwen's own Work360 evaluation, the average cost per task fell from $4.43 to $1.67 — a 62% cut against the previous generation, Qwen3.8-Max. That is a big claim, and it is worth unpacking carefully, because the interesting part of this release is not any single benchmark. It is how the model was built to be cheaper to run and harder to derail on long, messy, real-world jobs — and where the announcement still leaves questions unanswered.

articles.body: Coding Assistants vs AI Agents: Stop Mixing Them Up Use an AI coding assistant if you are writing code inside an IDE and a human still reviews each step. Use an AI agent builder if you are automating a workflow that spans business systems outside your codebase. Mixing the two terms makes buying and security reviews worse. Disclosure: This piece is from the ToolPotion Media Team. ToolPotion is our product. Adoption and revenue figures below come from our assistants vs agents comparison . Two jobs, two loops Coding assistant: sits in the editor, proposes completions or patches, waits for you. GitHub Copilot and Cursor are the familiar shape. You stay the decision-maker. The tool proposes; you dispose. Agent builder: you design a workflow once (triggers, logic, actions across apps).

articles.title: Every Plugin I Shipped Installed a TypeScript Compiler
articles.excerpt: I went looking for why my linter felt slow to start. I found a TypeScript compiler in node_modules — once per plugin, never asked for. My first theory was that I'd inherited it from @typescript-eslint…
articles.body: I went looking for why my linter felt slow to start. I found a TypeScript compiler in node_modules — once per plugin, never asked for. My first theory was that I'd inherited it from @typescript-eslint/utils . My second was that it was my own fault. Both were half right, which is why the first fix didn't work. Devkit at 1.0.0 : "peerDependencies" : { "typescript" : ">=4.0.0" , "get-tsconfig" : "^4.13.0" , "enhanced-resolve" : "^5.18.3" , "@typescript-eslint/utils" : "^8.46.2" } , "peerDependenciesMeta" : { "get-tsconfig" : { "optional" : true } , "enhanced-resolve" : { "optional" : true } } Four peers, two marked optional. npm 7+ auto-installs the ones that aren't ( npm/cli#4828 ).

articles.body: I run Prisma Reviews, a small API that returns customer reviews from 84 platforms in one JSON format. This post is not about the product. It is about three engineering problems that took most of our time: designing a schema that fits sources with very different shapes, keeping IDs stable so the same review never shows up twice, and testing the contract so that a change upstream does not quietly break clients downstream. Try Apidog today One thing first, because it shapes everything else: not every review source is an API. Of our 84 sources, 59 have an official API. The other 25 do not, and we read their public pages or feeds instead.

articles.title: My ESP32 gadget crashed every time it refreshed a token. The bug was in where the task's stack lived.
articles.excerpt: I've been building Ava, a personal desk gadget on a Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75" round AMOLED board, using Meta's open source Muse Gadgets SDK. The SDK gives you the firmware for pairing, a Bluetooth comp…
articles.body: I've been building Ava , a personal desk gadget on a Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75" round AMOLED board, using Meta's open source Muse Gadgets SDK . The SDK gives you the firmware for pairing, a Bluetooth companion, a display UI and a session with the Muse backend, and you bring the hardware. Everything worked, until the gadget hit its first token refresh. Then it crashed and rebooted. Every time. No memory corruption, no null pointer, nothing in my own code. The cause was which kind of RAM a single task's stack lived in . It's an easy one to miss on any ESP32 with PSRAM, so here's the whole story. The symptom The gadget pairs, connects and runs fine. When its session token needs refreshing, it asserts and reboots .

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. articles.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
articles.excerpt: SpaceX just made spaceflight history, catching the upper stage of its Starship megarocket when it returned to Earth. But Starship still has some pretty big boxes left to check.
articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.
